authoredPrompt: This figure is a ball-and-stick model of one tetraphosphorus trisulfide molecule, P4S3, drawn against a plain white background with no axes or scale. Four orange spheres labeled "P" and three smaller yellow spheres labeled "S" are joined by cylindrical bonds colored in halves, orange on the phosphorus end and yellow on the sulfur end. Three phosphorus atoms form a triangular base across the lower part of the model, drawn in perspective with one sphere at the left, one at the right, and one nearer the viewer at the bottom center; solid orange bonds connect all three directly to one another. A fourth phosphorus sits alone at the apex. Each sulfur bridges that apical phosphorus down to one basal phosphorus, placing the sulfurs at the left, right, and middle of the model, the central one drawn in front with its bond running straight down to the near basal atom. The whole is a closed cage in which every sulfur is two-coordinate and every phosphorus three-coordinate. Splitting each bond into two colors keeps the phosphorus-sulfur links distinct and leaves the three phosphorus-phosphorus bonds around the base unmistakable — direct P-P bonding of the kind that gives phosphorus an oxidation state unusual for a group 15 element.
authoredInteractions:
- Click a P-P base bond or a P-S bridge to highlight all bonds of that type, making clear that the molecule contains direct phosphorus-phosphorus bonding as well as phosphorus-sulfur links.
- Toggle between atom-count and coordination overlays: labels switch from P/S symbols to coordination numbers, making clear that each sulfur is two-coordinate while each phosphorus is three-coordinate.
authoredContext:
The phosphorus distills out of the furnace and is condensed into a solid or burned to form P4O10. The preparation of many other phosphorus compounds begins with P4O10. The acids and phosphates are useful as fertilizers and in the chemical industry. Other uses are in the manufacture of special alloys such as ferrophosphorus and phosphor bronze. Phosphorus is important in making pesticides, matches, and some plastics. Phosphorus is an active nonmetal. In compounds, phosphorus usually occurs in oxidation states of 3−, 3+, and 5+. Phosphorus exhibits oxidation numbers that are unusual for a group 15 element in compounds that contain phosphorus-phosphorus bonds; examples include diphosphorus tetrahydride, H2P-PH2, and tetraphosphorus trisulfide, P4S3, illustrated in the figure.

P4S3 is a component of the heads of strike-anywhere matches.

A ball-and-stick model is shown. Three orange atoms labeled “P” are single bonded together in a triangle shape. Each “P” is single bonded to yellow atoms labeled “S,” which are each single bonded to one other orange atom labeled “P.”
